questions.question: A bacterium keeps all of its genes on one long loop. In warm broth rich in food, it grows to about twice its length and splits across its middle into two cells, and some kinds can do this every 20 minutes. How do the genes of the two new cells compare with the genes of the first?
questions.answer: Both have the same genes as the first cell
choices: Both have the same genes as the first cell
Each has half of the first cell's genes
Each has a new mix of the first cell's genes
One has the old genes and one has new genes
questions.context: Before it splits, the bacterium copies its loop of genes, so each new cell gets a full copy, the same genes apart from rare copying mistakes. Nothing is halved and nothing is mixed: one parent makes two identical offspring, and at one split every 20 minutes, a single cell can become over a million in under seven hours.
questions.grade_note: NGSS MS-LS3-2 asks 7th graders to explain why asexual reproduction gives offspring the same genetic information as the parent, and a bacterium splitting in two is the first case the grade's line names.

questions.question: Baker's yeast is a one-celled fungus. While sugar and other food are plentiful, each cell buds: a small new cell swells from its side and breaks away. When food runs short, yeast can switch to a sexual way of reproducing and form spores. How can the switch help the yeast through hard times?
questions.answer: Its offspring vary, so some may suit the change
choices: Its offspring vary, so some may suit the change
Its offspring come faster, so more survive
Its offspring copy the parent, so none is weaker
Its offspring are stronger, so all survive
questions.context: Sexual reproduction mixes genes into new combinations, so the offspring differ from each other and from the parent, and when conditions change, some of them may cope better than the parent would. Budding is the faster way, but it only copies a parent suited to the good times; sexual offspring are not stronger by rule, since some mixes are better and some worse. Biologists still debate every reason sex persists, and in yeast the repair of damaged genes may matter too.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 7.13C and MS-LS3-2 compare the results of asexual and sexual reproduction, and a fungus that switches between them as conditions change shows when each one pays.

questions.question: A loaf of bread comes out of the oven, cools on a rack, and is sliced and sealed in a plastic bag. A week later, fuzzy patches of mould are spreading over several slices, though nothing mouldy ever touched the loaf. Where did the mould most likely come from?
questions.answer: Spores carried onto it by the air
choices: Spores carried onto it by the air
The bread itself as it went stale
Baker's yeast left alive in the bread
Bacteria in the bread turning into mould
questions.context: Mould spores are far too small to see and float through the air indoors and out; some settled on the bread as it cooled or was sliced, and each grew into a new mould, a copy of the one that shed it. Pier Antonio Micheli, an Italian botanist of the 1700s, set spores on slices of melon, grew the same kind of fungus, and argued that fungi do not spring from the food itself, as the old idea of spontaneous generation held. Yeast and bacteria are other microbes, and neither turns into mould.
questions.grade_note: Spores of moulds are one of the asexual ways the grade's line (G7.L5) names, and mould on bread is the case students meet at home.

questions.question: A gardener's best strawberry plant sends out runners, long stems that creep over the soil, and a small new plant takes root at the tip of each. Bees bring pollen to its flowers from the other plants in her bed, and she also sows the seeds from its berries. Which of the young plants carry exactly the parent's genes?
questions.answer: Only the plants from the runners
choices: Only the plants from the runners
Only the plants from the seeds
Both the runner plants and the seedlings
Neither the runner plants nor the seedlings
questions.context: A runner's plant grows from the parent's own stem, so it is a clone with exactly its genes, and growers spread a good strawberry this way, as potato growers plant pieces with eyes. Each seed formed when a cell from a grain of pollen joined an egg cell in the flower, so each seedling holds a new mix of genes, and garden strawberries grown from seed do not come true to their parent.
questions.grade_note: MS-LS3-2 contrasts the identical offspring of asexual reproduction with the varied offspring of sexual reproduction, and a strawberry plant makes both at once.

questions.question: A planarian is a small flatworm that glides over the stones of ponds and streams. In a laboratory, a biologist cuts one in two across its middle and keeps both pieces in clean pond water. What becomes of the two pieces over the next few weeks?
questions.answer: Each piece grows into a whole worm
choices: Each piece grows into a whole worm
Only the head piece grows a new tail
The two pieces heal back into one
Both pieces die within a few days
questions.context: A planarian's body is full of stem cells that can build any missing part, so the head piece grows a new tail and the tail piece a new head; a piece as small as 1/279th of a worm can regrow a whole one. Some planarians reproduce this way on their own, pinching in two across the middle, and each half becomes a worm with the same genes as the one parent.
questions.grade_note: Regeneration is one of the asexual ways the grade's line names, and the planarian is the textbook case of it.

questions.question: John Medley Wood, a botanist, found a single cycad, a cone-bearing plant, at the edge of a South African forest in 1895. It was a male, and no other wild plant of its kind has ever been found. Gardeners have since raised hundreds of plants from shoots that sprouted at its base. Why has none of them ever made a seed?
questions.answer: Every one is a clone of Wood's plant
choices: Every one is a clone of Wood's plant
Plants grown from shoots never make cones
Its seeds can form only in its home forest
The plants are still too young to seed
questions.context: Cycads grow as separate male and female plants, and a seed forms only when pollen from a male's cones reaches an ovule on a female's cones. Shoots from the base are clones, so all of the roughly 500 plants of Wood's cycad are males with the very same genes; the one at Kew Gardens, grown from a shoot sent in 1899, bore its first male cone in 2004. Drones searched the forest in 2022 and 2024, and no female has turned up.
questions.grade_note: The grade teaches that sexual reproduction joins cells from two parents (in cycads a male and a female plant, with cones) and that asexual offspring are copies; Wood's cycad shows both at once.

questions.question: The tassel at the top of a corn stalk sheds clouds of pollen. Each strand of silk on a young ear below is part of one tiny flower's pistil and leads down to one kernel-to-be. A gardener grows corn in a single long row, and many ears come out with gaps where no kernels formed. What most likely went wrong?
questions.answer: Too little pollen reached those silks
choices: Too little pollen reached those silks
Those silks needed insects to bring pollen
Too much pollen landed on those silks
Those silks got pollen from their own stalk
questions.context: Corn is pollinated by the wind, and a kernel grows only where a pollen grain lands on its silk and sends a tube down to the ovule. In a single row much of the pollen blows away from the ears, so many silks catch none, and garden guides advise a block of at least three or four short rows. Corn needs no insects, one grain is enough for each silk, and a stalk's own pollen can make kernels too.
questions.grade_note: The grade's line teaches the pistil and pollination by wind, and NGSS MS-LS1-4 asks how plant structures affect the odds of reproducing; corn's tassels and silks are the standard wind-pollinated case.

questions.question: A wildflower blooms by day, hanging long red tubes with plenty of watery nectar hidden deep inside. It gives off no scent at all. Which animal does it most likely depend on to carry its pollen?
choices: A hummingbird
A nectar-feeding bat
A night-flying moth
A pollen-eating beetle
questions.context: Flowers pollinated by birds are typically red or orange, tube-shaped, full of watery nectar and scentless, since birds find flowers by sight and have a poor sense of smell. Moth and bat flowers mostly open at night and give off strong scents, and beetle flowers are open bowls with strong smells and little nectar. Such patterns are tendencies, not rules, and bees visit some red flowers too.
questions.grade_note: MS-LS1-4 asks how a flower's structures raise its odds of being pollinated, and matching a flower to its pollinator, birds included, applies the grade's line on pollination by insects and birds.

questions.question: To a person, a meadow buttercup's petals look plain, glossy yellow. A camera that records ultraviolet light shows something more: each petal is pale at its tip and dark toward the centre of the flower. What job does the dark pattern most likely do?
questions.answer: It guides bees to the nectar
choices: It guides bees to the nectar
It warns leaf-eating insects away
It draws moths to it at night
It soaks up light to make food
questions.context: Bees see ultraviolet light, which people cannot, and the dark patch marks the flower's centre, where the nectar lies: a nectar guide, which helps a bee find its reward quickly and brush against pollen as it feeds. Bees cannot see red, one reason bee flowers are so often blue or yellow. Moths seek pale, scented flowers at night, and a plant makes its food in its green leaves, not its petals.
questions.grade_note: MS-LS1-4 names the colours and patterns that draw pollinating insects to flowers, and the petals' job of attracting pollinators is on the grade's line; an ultraviolet nectar guide is a case students can reason about.

questions.question: A gardener splits a green pea pod along its seam, and a row of peas sits inside, each joined to the pod by a short stalk. Cooks call the pod a vegetable, but to a botanist it is a fruit, and the peas are its seeds. Which part of the pea flower grew into the pod?
choices: The ovary
The petals
The stamens
The sepals
questions.context: After pollen fertilizes the egg cells in the ovules, the ovary at the base of the pistil swells into the fruit and the ovules ripen into seeds. That is why tomatoes and cucumbers are fruits too, sweet or not. Petals draw pollinators, stamens make pollen, and the sepals wrapped the young bud; none of them becomes the pod.
questions.grade_note: The grade's line carries the flower's parts through to seed and fruit, and that a fruit is a ripened ovary is the fact behind calling a pea pod a fruit.
